solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Plant's beginning to flop down in secluded spot

parts.note: a corner is a tucked-away spot

explanation.surface: A plant wilts and droops in some quiet corner of the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Down’ reads as the direction of the flop, but it is a separate piece meaning depressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: this blue wildflower of cornfields is one of countless plants.

clue.text: Raging egomaniac or what?

indicators.note: something raging is wild and out of order, so the letters are thrown about

parts.note: the nine letters of EGOMANIAC rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a raging egomaniac could be anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Or what?’ reads as a rhetorical tag on the surface; alone, ‘what?’ is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: both are informal requests to repeat something you didn’t catch.

clue.text: Master again back around the Spanish Main, at last

indicators.note: to go around something is to encircle it
what comes at last is the end, so take Main’s final letter

parts.note: the back of something is its rear

explanation.surface: A pirate returns to master the Spanish Main once more.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spanish Main was the Caribbean coast of Spain’s empire, but here ‘Main’ gives only its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: learn means master, and the RE- prefix supplies ‘again’.

clue.text: Sweethearts have tête-à-tête?

parts.note: to have a meal is to eat it

explanation.surface: Two sweethearts sit down for an intimate chat.
explanation.walkthrough: A tête-à-tête is also an S-shaped sofa where two people sit facing each other, so the ‘chat’ is really furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A less familiar sense: tête-à-tête also names a two-person sofa, the same furniture as this small settee for couples.

clue.text: Whilst hiking, fun somehow turns into false optimism

indicators.note: done somehow means done in some unspecified way, so the letters come out in a new order

explanation.surface: A walker’s cheerful mood on the trail turns out to be self-delusion.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder spans three words and a comma, which is how fifteen letters hide in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive paraphrase: believing what you wish were true is hope without grounds.

clue.text: Accent in Kent town almost grasped by soldiers

indicators.note: almost the whole word means stopping just short, so HYTHE loses its last letter
something grasped is held in the hands

parts.note: HYTHE, a town on the Kent coast, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Soldiers notice a local accent in a Kentish town.
explanation.walkthrough: Hythe is a small coastal town in Kent, in south-east England. ‘Accent’ suggests speech, but it is the musical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical sense from music and verse: accent is the stress pattern that makes a beat.

clue.text: About a thousand following live stream

explanation.surface: Some thousand people follow a live broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Live stream’ reads as one online phrase; ‘live’ is BE and ‘stream’ is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional word: in northern England a brook or small watercourse is called a beck.

clue.text: Dance leader, first-class, picked up flower

indicators.note: something picked up is lifted

parts.note: a flower is something that flows: a river, here the Avon

explanation.surface: A leading dancer, top of the class, picks up a bloom thrown on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Flower’ is a crossword staple for river: something that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: this Brazilian style related to the samba is one kind of dance.

clue.text: Informal exchange with Middle Eastern state set up in country house

parts.note: a chat is an informal talk

indicators.note: to set something up is to raise it

explanation.surface: A casual conversation with a Gulf state is arranged at a country estate.
explanation.walkthrough: The UAE is the United Arab Emirates, a Gulf state; its initials turned upward make a French-looking ending.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowed word: French uses it for a large rural mansion or castle.

clue.text: Chaps screening short film about tropical islands

indicators.note: to screen is to shield or hide behind
to turn about is to face the other way
a short word falls short of its full length

explanation.surface: Some men screen a brief documentary about tropical islands.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Screening’ suggests showing the film, which is exactly the sense to set aside: here it means shielding.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific place: this Indian Ocean nation is a chain of tropical coral atolls.

clue.text: An agreeable sort, bellboy finally succeeded in turning handle

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
what comes finally comes last, so take bellboy’s last letter
turning round means facing the other way

parts.note: s = succeeded, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A cheerful bellboy finally manages to turn a door handle.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Handle’ is a door fitting on the surface and slang for a name in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful paraphrase: someone who always says yes is agreeable in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Nerd wastes no liquor

indicators.note: to waste something is to lose it

parts.note: in Britain an anorak is an obsessive nerd

explanation.surface: A geek refuses to let any drink go to waste.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘No liquor’ reads as a phrase; ‘no’ is the letters taken out. British slang calls a train-spotting type an anorak, after the hooded jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: this anise spirit of the Middle East and Asia is a kind of strong drink.

clue.text: Simple versions of the ad, edited to a certain degree

indicators.note: something true only to a certain degree is partly so, and only part of the phrase is used

explanation.surface: Dumbed-down cuts of an advert have been trimmed a bit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about editing an ad, which makes ‘edited’ look like an anagram signal; the answer is simply sitting in the words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: simple in the sense of simple-minded, lacking good sense.

clue.text: A comrade comes across military groups — heartless, or fair target?

indicators.note: without a heart means without a middle, so UNITS loses its central I
to come across is to span from one side to the other

explanation.surface: A fellow soldier stumbles on some heartless army units.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aunt Sally is a British fairground game in which you throw sticks at a dummy’s head; figuratively, anyone set up to be criticised.
explanation.definitionFit: A British fairground game: the wooden dummy you throw at is literally a target at a fair.

clue.text: Keen swimmer pulls in Resistance soldier

indicators.note: to pull something in is to draw it inside

parts.note: the tench is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic swimmer hauls a Resistance fighter aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Resistance soldier’ reads as one wartime figure but splits into two pieces; ‘Keen’ is sharp, not eager.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of sharp: a keen or cutting remark is incisive.

clue.text: Trade union engaged in head count

indicators.note: to be engaged in something is to be occupied inside it

explanation.surface: A trade union carries out a head count of its members.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Head count’ reads as one term; ‘head’ is a piece of wordplay and ‘count’ the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal British phrasal verb for adding numbers together to reach a total.

clue.text: As such, always interrupting — go on?

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something

parts.note: per se = as such, in itself

explanation.surface: Someone who always cuts in is urged to carry on regardless.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase per se means ‘as such’ or ‘in itself’; the question mark flags that ‘go on?’ is an encouragement rather than a question.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to go on in the sense of keep going despite difficulty.

clue.text: Shabby journalist turned up and moved quietly around island

indicators.note: something turned up is flipped upward
to go around is to encircle

explanation.surface: A scruffy reporter arrives and tiptoes round an island.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Turned up’ looks like ‘arrived’; in a down clue it flips the letters upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: worn out and run-down by age or neglect, as a shabby building is.

clue.text: Part of staircase requires fresh coat of enamel

indicators.note: a coat covers the outside of something, so the coat of enamel is its outside letters

explanation.surface: A staircase needs repainting with a fresh coat of enamel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes ‘coat’ literal paint; here it wraps a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical term: the upright post supporting a stair’s handrail at the foot or a turn.

clue.text: Reserve electronic weapon on ship

indicators.note: one thing on another sits above it

explanation.surface: A navy sets aside an electronic weapon for one of its ships.
explanation.walkthrough: A straight charade, read top to bottom; ‘on’ matters only because this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to set aside money or goods for a particular purpose.

clue.text: Mark? He's excited about old English craftsman

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up, so the letters are shaken into a new order
to be about something is to surround it, so the rearranged letters go around OE

explanation.surface: Mark gets excited about an old English craftsman.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Mark?’ looks like a name being asked about; it is anagram fodder along with ‘He’s’.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a cobbler who makes footwear by hand is one kind of craftsman.

clue.text: Man possessing skill in motorsport?

indicators.note: to possess something is to hold it

parts.note: a man in chess, such as the king

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a man is any good at motor racing.
explanation.walkthrough: Chess pieces are called men, so ‘man’ can be a specific piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: racing small open go-karts round a track is one kind of motorsport.

clue.text: Safe to cuddle small hound

indicators.note: to cuddle is to wrap your arms around

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: It is safe to hug a little dog.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Hound’ looks like a dog to cuddle; it is the verb. Safe-crackers were once ‘peter-men’.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as verbs: to harass someone with persistent demands.

clue.text: One removes stains from front of coat that's covered in red and nearly ruined

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter
something ruined is wrecked, so RED and NEARLY are smashed into a new order
something covered in a layer sits inside it

explanation.surface: A coat splashed with red is nearly ruined, so off it goes to be cleaned.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Nearly’ looks like a signal to shorten a word; it is whole letters for rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the business that cleans clothes with solvents is where stains are taken out.

clue.text: Press retreating, some begrudgingly

indicators.note: to retreat is to go backwards, so the letters run in reverse
some of a word is only part of it, so the answer sits inside begrudgingly

explanation.surface: The newspapers pull back, some of them grudgingly.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Press’ looks like the newspapers in retreat; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as verbs: to push someone insistently to act.

clue.text: Rock band, half-cut, opening in strange key

indicators.note: a word half cut has lost half its length
the opening of a word is where it begins

parts.note: the Alt key on a keyboard

explanation.surface: A drunken rock band opens its set in an odd key.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Rock band’ and ‘half-cut’ (British for tipsy) paint a gig; ‘Rock’ is the definition and ‘key’ is on a keyboard, not a stave.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: this dark volcanic stone is one of the commonest rocks.

clue.text: Unpolished, one small thing holds ring in place

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside your grasp

parts.note: a mite is a tiny thing

explanation.surface: A rough-cut stone: one small setting holds a ring in place.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest, one inside the other; ‘in place’ looks like a fixing, but ‘place’ is its own abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: unpolished manners lack refinement, just as rude ones do.

clue.text: Fringe drops penultimate comedy routine

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, and the penultimate letter is the second-to-last, so R goes

parts.note: to skirt is to lie along the fringe or edge of something

explanation.surface: A fringe show cuts its second-last comedy routine.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Fringe’ suggests the comedy festival fringe; it means edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a short comic sketch performed as part of a show.

clue.text: Large gathering assembled in part of square

indicators.note: things assembled are put together in a new arrangement, so the letters are rebuilt

parts.note: L = large, as in clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A huge crowd assembles in a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Large gathering’ reads as one crowd; ‘Large’ gives only L, and ‘square’ is the geometric shape, not a plaza.
explanation.definitionFit: A geometric fact: every corner of a square is a ninety-degree angle.
